question: A 30-year-old man presents with a single pale patch on his forearm. Which bedside finding must be checked first, and why?

answers.text: Test light-touch sensation on the patch — loss of sensation (anaesthesia) points to leprosy, a treatable infection that must not be missed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. On every hypopigmented or depigmented patch, the mandatory first test is for sensation. Leprosy produces hypopigmented patches that are anaesthetic (impaired light touch and temperature), whereas vitiligo has entirely normal sensation. Missing the anaesthesia means missing a treatable, notifiable infection.

answers.text: Examine for scaling — the presence of scale confirms a fungal infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While fine powdery scale may suggest pityriasis versicolor, the clinical priority for any pale patch is to exclude leprosy by testing sensation, not to look for scale.

answers.text: Check for bilateral symmetry — asymmetric patches are always benign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Asymmetry alone does not determine benignity. Both segmental vitiligo and leprosy can present unilaterally. Sensory testing is the critical discriminator.

answers.text: Apply pressure to blanch the patch — capillary refill time distinguishes the cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Capillary refill and blanching are irrelevant to the differential of pigmentary disorders. Sensory testing is the decisive and most consequential bedside test.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cardinal rule for any pale patch: TEST SENSATION FIRST. Leprosy = hypopigmented and anaesthetic; vitiligo = depigmented with normal sensation. This single test separates a cosmetic pigmentary condition from a treatable infectious disease.

Essential habit: test sensation on every pale patch. Normal sensation favours vitiligo; impaired sensation demands evaluation for leprosy — a treatable, notifiable infection with serious consequences if missed.
